intro: This unit introduces Michael S. Heiser (1963–2023). He was a scholar who read the Hebrew Bible in its first language. He also read other old languages, like Greek and Ugaritic. His big idea was to read the Bible the way its first readers did.

You will meet the Hebrew word elohim. Heiser said it names beings whose home is the spirit world. Then you will read the Bible's council scenes. They are in Psalm 82, Psalm 89, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2 and Isaiah 6. Heiser called this picture the divine council, God's heavenly court.

Readers do not all agree about these passages. You will learn Heiser's reading and at least one other reading. By the end, you will be able to explain a passage, name who said what, and compare two readings fairly.
bigQuestion: What did Michael Heiser notice about God's heavenly council, and how do other readers see the same passages?

title: Meeting Michael Heiser and the Divine Council
years: The Scholar and His Big Idea

chapters.title: A Scholar Who Read the Old Languages
chapters.bigQuestion: How can reading the Bible in its first languages change what a reader notices?

story.title: The Verse That Stopped Her
story.kicker: A college student reads one short verse in Hebrew and has to read it again.
paragraphs: Nina sat in the college library with a thick book open in front of her. It was a Hebrew Bible. The letters ran from right to left. She had studied Hebrew for one year. Now her teacher had asked the class to read Psalm 82 on their own.

The first verse was short. Nina found the word for God. Then she found the same word again, a few words later. The first time, it meant God. The second time, it seemed to mean many beings. The verse seemed to say that God stands in a council and judges among the gods.

Nina frowned. She checked her dictionary. She checked her grammar notes. The word was elohim both times. The grammar showed that the first one was one being and the second one was many. She raised her hand and asked, "Who are the other elohim?"

Her teacher smiled. "That is a very old question," she said. "Readers have answered it in more than one way. One scholar, Michael Heiser, wrote that this psalm surprised him too when he read it in Hebrew. It changed how he read the whole Bible."

Nina wrote the question at the top of her notebook. She wanted to know how one old word could mean more than one thing. She also wanted to know what the first people who heard this psalm thought it meant.
story.think: Have you ever read a word that meant something different from what you expected? What helped you figure it out?

lessons.title: A Life Spent Reading
lessons.mainIdea: Michael Heiser (1963–2023) was a scholar who studied the Hebrew Bible and the languages of the ancient world.
reading: Michael S. Heiser was born in 1963 and died in 2023. He was a *scholar*. A scholar is a person who studies one subject very deeply. Heiser's subject was the *Hebrew Bible*. That is the collection of books Jewish readers call the Tanakh and Christians call the Old Testament.

In 2004 Heiser earned a PhD from the University of Wisconsin–Madison. A PhD is the highest degree a university gives. Madison is a few hours' drive north of Chicago. His studies there were in the Hebrew Bible and in Semitic languages. Semitic languages are a family of languages that includes Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic.

For his PhD, Heiser wrote a long paper called a dissertation. It was about the divine council, the idea that God has a heavenly court. He kept studying that idea for the rest of his life. It became the center of his best-known books.

words.d: a person who studies one subject very deeply and writes about it
the books Jewish readers call the Tanakh and Christians call the Old Testament
the highest degree a university gives, earned by years of study and a long research paper

lessons.title: Old Languages, New Eyes
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the Bible's first languages, like Hebrew and Greek, and related languages like Ugaritic.
reading: Most people read the Bible in a *translation*. A translation moves words from one language into another. The Hebrew Bible was first written mostly in Hebrew, with a few parts in Aramaic. The New Testament was first written in Greek.

Heiser learned to read these first languages. He also read *Ugaritic*. That is the language of Ugarit, an old city on the coast of what is now Syria. Its clay tablets were written around 1300 BCE. Ugaritic is a close cousin of Hebrew, so it can help explain Hebrew words.

Why does this matter? Every translator has to make choices. One Hebrew word might become two different English words in two places. Heiser wanted to see the words before those choices were made. Then he could ask what the first readers heard.

words.d: words moved from one language into another, like Hebrew into English
the language of the old city of Ugarit in Syria, a close cousin of Hebrew
a language related to Hebrew; a few parts of the Hebrew Bible are written in it

check.why: The New Testament was first written in Greek.

check.q: Why is Ugaritic helpful to someone reading Hebrew?

check.why: Ugaritic is closely related to Hebrew, so its words can shed light on Hebrew words.

check.q: Why did Heiser want to read the Bible in its first languages?
choices: To see the words before a translator made choices
To avoid reading the Bible at all
check.why: Translators must make choices; Heiser wanted to see the words before those choices were made.

lessons.title: Books and a Podcast
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser shared his ideas in books like The Unseen Realm and Supernatural and on the Naked Bible Podcast.
reading: In 2015 Heiser published *The Unseen Realm*. The full title calls it a book about recovering the supernatural worldview of the Bible. It is long and full of notes. It explains his ideas about God, the divine council and the spirit world.

The same year, he published *Supernatural*. It covers many of the same ideas in a shorter and easier way. Later he wrote books called Angels (2018) and Demons (2020). Each one looks at what the Bible and other old texts say about a group of spirit beings.

From 2014 to 2023, Heiser also hosted the Naked Bible Podcast. On it, he talked through books of the Bible, one passage at a time. The name points to his goal. He wanted to look at the Bible itself, without extra layers of ideas that were added much later.

words.d: Heiser's 2015 book about the Bible's view of God and the spirit world
Heiser's shorter 2015 book that explains the ideas of The Unseen Realm more simply
a talk show you can listen to online, in episodes

look.title: Long Book, Short Book
look.text: Heiser wrote one big book, The Unseen Realm (2015), with many notes for scholars. In the same year he wrote Supernatural (2015), a shorter book on many of the same ideas for everyday readers.
look.prompt: Why might a writer tell the same ideas in two books of different sizes? Who is each book for?

check.why: The Unseen Realm was published in 2015.

lessons.title: The First Readers' World
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser's big idea was to read the Bible the way its first readers would have understood it.
reading: Think of a text message from today. Someone reading it 3,000 years from now might be confused. What is a phone? What does a smiley face mean? They would need to learn about our world first. Heiser said the Bible is like that too.

The first readers of the Hebrew Bible lived in the *ancient Near East*. That is the old name for lands like Israel, Egypt, Syria and Iraq long ago. People there had their own ideas about kings, gods, temples and the sky. Bible writers used words those readers knew.

Heiser's big idea was simple to say. Read the Bible the way its first readers did, not through ideas that came much later. He called this reading the Bible in its own *context*. Context means the time, place and ideas around a text.

words.d: the old lands of Egypt, Israel, Syria, Iraq and nearby places, long ago
the time, place and ideas around a text that help explain what it means

look.title: A Note From Long Ago
look.text: Imagine someone in the year 5000 finds a note that says: "Meet me by the L after school." In Chicago today, most people know the L is the city's train. A reader far in the future would not know that.
look.prompt: What would the future reader need to learn to understand the note? How is this like reading an old book like the Bible?

check.q: What was Heiser's big idea about reading the Bible?
choices: Read it as a science textbook
Read it the way its first readers understood it
Read it only in modern slang
check.why: Heiser said to read the Bible in its own context, as its first readers did.

check.q: What does context mean?
choices: The time, place and ideas around a text
check.why: Context is the time, place and ideas that surround a text.

check.q: Which lands were part of the ancient Near East?
check.why: The ancient Near East means old lands like Egypt, Israel, Syria and Iraq.

lessons.title: Clues From Ugarit
lessons.mainIdea: Clay tablets from Ugarit describe a council of gods, which helped Heiser read council scenes in the Bible.
reading: In 1928 a farmer in Syria hit a stone while plowing. It led to the ruins of Ugarit. Beginning in 1929, diggers found thousands of *clay tablets* there. The tablets were written in wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay.

Some Ugarit tablets tell stories about their gods. In them, the high god El leads a gathering of gods, called his assembly. The gods in it are called the sons of El. Some of the same kinds of words for a heavenly gathering also appear in the Hebrew Bible.

Heiser used these tablets as clues. He did not say the Bible copied Ugarit. He said Bible writers used words their neighbors knew, but gave them new meaning. In the Bible, he pointed out, Israel's God sits at the head of the council instead of El or Baal.

words.d: flat pieces of clay with writing pressed into them while wet, used in the ancient Near East
a gathering of members who meet together, like a council

look.title: Two Gatherings Side by Side
look.text: Ugarit tablets: the high god El leads an assembly of gods called the sons of El. Psalm 82 (Hebrew Bible): God stands in a council and judges among the gods.
look.prompt: What is the same in these two pictures? What is different about who is in charge?

check.q: What did diggers find at Ugarit?
check.why: Diggers found thousands of clay tablets at Ugarit beginning in 1929.

check.q: In the Ugarit tablets, who leads the assembly of gods?
check.why: The Ugarit texts show the high god El leading an assembly of gods.

check.q: How did Heiser use the Ugarit tablets?
choices: As proof that the Bible copied Ugarit
As a new book of the Bible

check.why: He saw them as clues, and said Bible writers used familiar words but gave them new meaning.

lessons.title: Checking Big Claims
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser checked popular claims against the ancient texts, and he rejected ideas like ancient aliens.
reading: Some books and videos make big claims about the Bible. One claim says that space aliens visited the ancient world. Another says giants built the pyramids. These claims often use old words from ancient texts.

Heiser read those same old texts in their first languages. He wrote that the ancient-alien claims did not match what the texts really say. He said the claims often used words in ways the ancient writers never did. He asked readers to check before they believed a claim.

You can check claims too. First, ask where a claim comes from. Next, find the actual text it points to. Then read what the text says in its own context. A good reader looks at the evidence before deciding.

words.d: something a person says is true, which may or may not have evidence
facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: A video says: "An old text proves aliens built a city." A careful reader asks three questions. Which text? What does it actually say? What did the words mean to the people who wrote them?
look.prompt: Pick one of the three questions. Why does it help you check the claim?

check.q: What did Heiser say about ancient-alien claims?
choices: They came from the Book of Psalms
They did not match what the ancient texts really say
check.why: Heiser rejected ancient-alien claims because they did not fit the texts.

check.q: What is a good first step to check a claim?
choices: Believe it if it sounds exciting
Ask where the claim comes from
check.why: The reading says to begin by asking where a claim comes from.

check.q: What does evidence mean?
choices: Facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits
check.why: Evidence is the facts or texts used to test a claim.

lessons.title: One Word, Many Beings
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word elohim can mean Israel's God, and it is also used for other beings from the spirit world.
reading: The Hebrew word *elohim* appears about 2,600 times in the Hebrew Bible. Most of the time it means Israel's God. Genesis 1:1 uses it: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." That is the King James Version of 1611.

But elohim is used for others too. Psalm 82:1 uses it for the beings in God's council. First Kings 11:33 uses it for the god of the Moabites, a neighboring people. Psalm 8:5 says humans were made a little lower than the elohim. An old Greek translation turned that word into angels.

So one word points to many beings. Heiser said this can surprise English readers. In English, God with a capital G is a name for one being. In Hebrew, elohim is a wider word. Readers use the rest of the sentence to see which being is meant.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for Israel's God and also for other beings of the spirit world
a people who lived east of the Dead Sea, neighbors of ancient Israel

look.title: Five Uses of One Word
look.text: Genesis 1:1: elohim created the heaven and the earth. Psalm 82:1: God judges among the elohim. 1 Kings 11:33: the elohim of the Moabites. Psalm 8:5: humans made a little lower than the elohim. Deuteronomy 10:17: the LORD is the elohim of the elohim, God of gods.
look.prompt: In which of these does the word mean Israel's God? In which does it mean other beings? What clues helped you?

check.q: What does elohim mean most of the time in the Hebrew Bible?
check.why: Most of its uses refer to Israel's God, as in Genesis 1:1.

check.q: In 1 Kings 11:33, elohim is used for whom?
check.why: First Kings 11:33 uses elohim for the god of the Moabites.

check.q: An old Greek translation turned elohim in Psalm 8:5 into which word?
check.why: The old Greek translation of Psalm 8:5 says angels where the Hebrew has elohim.

lessons.title: Where, Not What
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser said elohim tells where a being lives, in the spirit world, not what kind of being it is.
reading: How can one word fit so many beings? Heiser gave an answer in The Unseen Realm (2015). He said elohim is a word about *residence*. Residence means where someone lives. An elohim, he said, is a being whose home is the spirit world.

Think of the word Illinoisan. It means a person who lives in Illinois. A baby, a teacher and a farmer can all be Illinoisans. The word tells you where they live. It does not tell you what job they do or how strong they are.

Heiser read elohim that way. Israel's God is an elohim, because his home is the spirit world. The beings of his council are elohim too. The word alone, Heiser said, does not make them equal. Other scholars explain the word in other ways, and they still discuss it.

words.d: the place where someone lives
the unseen world the Bible describes, where God and heavenly beings are said to live

look.title: Heiser on the Word Elohim
look.text: Heiser explains that elohim is a word for any being whose home is the spirit world. The word tells where a being lives. It does not tell us what the being is like or how powerful it is.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015), paraphrased
look.prompt: How is the word elohim, as Heiser explains it, like the word Illinoisan?

check.q: According to Heiser, what does elohim tell you about a being?
check.why: Heiser said elohim is about residence: the spirit world is its home.

check.q: Why does the reading use the word Illinoisan?
choices: It names people by where they live, not what they are like
It means a kind of angel
check.why: Illinoisan tells where a person lives, just as Heiser said elohim tells where a being lives.

check.q: What does residence mean?
check.why: Residence means where someone lives.

lessons.title: None Like Israel's God
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser said Israel's God is unique: other elohim exist in the Bible's picture, but none is like him.
reading: If there are many elohim, is Israel's God just one among equals? Heiser said no. He pointed to verses that compare God to the other elohim. Exodus 15:11 asks who among the gods is like the LORD. Psalm 86:8 says there is none like him among the gods.

Heiser said Israel's God is *unique*. Unique means one of a kind. In the Bible's picture, Heiser explained, God made the other heavenly beings. They serve under him. He rules over them all, like a king far above his court.

Heiser liked to put it this way. Israel's God is an elohim, but no other elohim is Israel's God. The word they share is like a home address. The Being at the head of the council is still, he said, in a class of his own.

words.d: one of a kind; nothing else is like it
how many English Bibles show YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God

look.title: Who Is Like You?
look.text: After crossing the sea, Moses and the people sing to the LORD. They ask: who among the gods is like you? Who is so holy and so wonderful, doing amazing things?
look.cite: Exodus 15:11, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What does this song say about how Israel's God compares to the gods?

check.q: What does unique mean?
check.why: Unique means nothing else is like it.

check.q: Which verse asks who among the gods is like the LORD?
check.why: Exodus 15:11, the song after crossing the sea, asks this question.

check.q: How did Heiser describe Israel's God compared to other elohim?
choices: He made them and rules over them all
He is one of many equals
He is the youngest of them
check.why: Heiser said God made the other heavenly beings and rules over them.

lessons.title: One or Many? Context Tells
lessons.mainIdea: Elohim looks plural, but the words around it show whether it means one being or many.
reading: In Hebrew, the ending -im often makes a word plural, meaning more than one. Elohim ends in -im. So how can it mean one God? Hebrew readers look at the words around it. When elohim goes with a verb for one person, it means one being.

Genesis 1:1 uses elohim with a verb for one person. So it means one God, who creates. But in Psalm 82:1, the second elohim is in a phrase that needs more than one. The verse speaks of God judging in the midst of the elohim. You can only stand in the midst of many.

English has a word like this. The word *sheep* can mean one sheep or many sheep. You know which one from the sentence. "The sheep is eating" means one. "The sheep are eating" means many. Heiser read elohim with the same kind of clue.

words.d: meaning more than one
an English word that can mean one animal or many; the sentence tells you which

look.title: Find the Clue
look.text: Sentence A: The sheep is in the barn. Sentence B: The sheep are in the barn. Psalm 82:1 (retold): God stands in the council; he judges in the midst of the elohim.
look.prompt: Which word in Sentence A and B tells you one or many? In Psalm 82:1, which words tell you the second elohim means many?

check.q: What does the ending -im often do to a Hebrew word?
check.why: The Hebrew ending -im often marks a plural.

check.q: How do readers know elohim means one God in Genesis 1:1?
choices: It is in a different book
It goes with a verb for one person
check.why: In Genesis 1:1 elohim goes with a verb for one person, so it means one God.

check.q: Which English word works like elohim, meaning one or many?
check.why: Sheep can mean one or many; the sentence shows which, as with elohim.

chapters.title: God's Council in Heaven
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the Bible's council scenes show about how God rules, as Heiser and other readers see them?

story.title: A Field Trip to City Hall
story.kicker: A fourth-grade class watches a city council meeting, and one student remembers a psalm.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz's fourth-grade class rode the bus to City Hall. They sat in rows at the back of a big room. At the front was a long curved table. The mayor sat in the middle. Council members sat on each side, with name signs in front of them.

The mayor called the meeting to order. A council member spoke about fixing a park. Another asked about the cost. A woman from the town came to the microphone and shared an idea. The mayor listened to everyone. Then the council voted, and the mayor read the result.
On the bus ride home, Sam looked out the window. "That was like a picture I read in the Psalms," he said. "In Psalm 82, God stands in a council. There are others there too, and God is in charge."

Ms. Ortiz nodded. "Some Bible readers call that the divine council," she said. "Michael Heiser wrote a lot about it. He thought the Bible shows God like a king with a court. Other readers see Psalm 82 in another way. We can look at both."
Sam thought about the mayor. The mayor did not need the council members to be the mayor. But the mayor still worked with them. He wondered why a king, or God, would have a council at all.
story.think: Why might a leader who is in charge still choose to work with a group of helpers?

lessons.title: Psalm 82: God Judges the Gods
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 82 shows God standing in a divine council and judging the elohim for being unfair.
reading: Psalm 82 is only eight verses long. It opens with a scene. God stands in the *divine council*. That means a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head. In the middle of them, God judges. The Hebrew calls the members elohim, which English Bibles often translate as gods.

Then God speaks. He asks how long they will judge unfairly. He tells them to protect the poor, the weak and children with no parents. But the members have not done it. The psalm says they do not understand and they walk in darkness.

God says he called them gods and sons of the Most High. But now, he says, they will die like humans. The psalm ends with a prayer. The writer asks God to rise up and judge the earth, because all the nations belong to him.

words.d: a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head, like a king's court
a title for Israel's God that shows he is above all others
to decide what is fair and right, and to say who has done wrong

look.title: Psalm 82 in Simple Words
look.text: God stands in the council. He judges among the gods. He says: How long will you judge unfairly? Protect the weak and the poor. I said you are gods, children of the Most High. But you will die like humans. Rise up, O God, and judge the earth. All the nations are yours.
look.cite: Psalm 82:1–8, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What does God want the members of the council to do? What have they done instead?

check.q: Where does God stand at the start of Psalm 82?
check.why: Psalm 82:1 says God stands in the council and judges among the elohim.

check.q: What does God tell the council members to do?
choices: Protect the poor and the weak
check.why: In Psalm 82:3–4 God tells them to defend the poor, the weak and children without parents.

check.q: How does Psalm 82 end?
choices: With a song about the sea
With a prayer for God to judge the earth
check.why: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise and judge the earth, because the nations are his.

lessons.title: The Assembly of the Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 89:5–7 describes an assembly of holy ones in the heavens, where no one compares to God.
reading: Psalm 89 is a long song of praise. Verses 5 to 7 describe a gathering in the heavens. The heavens praise God. The Hebrew calls the gathering the *assembly of the holy ones*. Holy ones is a name for heavenly beings who belong to God.

The psalm asks two questions. Who in the skies can compare to the LORD? Who among the sons of God is like him? The answer the psalm expects is no one. It says God is greatly respected in the council of the holy ones.

Heiser used this psalm to explain Psalm 82. Psalm 89 clearly places the council in the heavens, not on earth. He argued that the council in Psalm 82 is the same kind of heavenly gathering. He also noted that God is shown far above every member.

words.d: a phrase in Psalm 89 for the heavenly beings gathered around God
a name for heavenly beings who belong to God and serve him
a phrase the Hebrew Bible uses for heavenly beings in God's council

look.title: Who Is Like the LORD?
look.text: The heavens praise your wonders, LORD, and the holy ones praise your faithfulness. Who in the skies can compare to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like him? In the council of the holy ones, God is greatly honored.
look.cite: Psalm 89:5–7, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: Where does this council meet? What does the psalm say about God compared to the holy ones?

check.q: Where does Psalm 89 place the assembly of the holy ones?
check.why: Psalm 89:5–7 places the gathering in the heavens and the skies.

check.q: What answer does Psalm 89 expect to 'Who is like the LORD?'
check.why: The psalm's questions expect the answer that no one compares to God.

check.q: How did Heiser use Psalm 89 to explain Psalm 82?
choices: It shows Psalm 82 is about fish
It proves Psalm 82 was written in Greek
It shows there is no council
It shows the council is a heavenly gathering
check.why: Heiser argued that Psalm 89 places the council in heaven, so Psalm 82's council is heavenly too.

lessons.title: Like a King's Court
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser said God has a council like a king's court, not because he needs help, but because he chooses to share his work.
reading: In the ancient world, a king sat on a throne. Around him stood his court. These were officials and messengers who carried out his plans. The Bible often pictures God as a king on a throne. Heiser said the divine council is God's heavenly court.

Does God need a council? Heiser said no. In his reading, God is all-powerful and does not need anyone. But God chooses to include others in his work. Heiser described the council as God's heavenly family, beings he made to share in what he does.

Heiser also saw a link to people. He wrote that God wanted a family on earth too, made of humans. Just as the council shares God's work in heaven, humans were made to share his work on earth. Later units look closely at that idea.

words.d: the officials and helpers who stand around a king and carry out his plans
a special chair where a king sits to rule

look.title: Councils in Illinois Today
look.cite: City of Chicago and Illinois General Assembly; U.S. Constitution
look.prompt: Each of these groups works together to make choices. Which is the largest? Which is the smallest?

check.q: According to Heiser, why does God have a council?
choices: Because he chooses to share his work
Because a king in Ugarit told him to
check.why: Heiser said God does not need help but chooses to include others in his work.

check.q: What is a king's court?
choices: The officials and helpers around a king
check.why: A court is the group of officials and messengers who serve a king.

check.q: What did Heiser call the divine council?
check.why: Heiser described the council as God's heavenly family who share in his work.

lessons.title: Micaiah Sees the Throne
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Kings 22, the prophet Micaiah describes God on his throne asking the host of heaven for a plan.
reading: First Kings 22 tells about King Ahab of Israel. He wanted to go to war at a town called Ramoth-gilead. About 400 of his prophets told him he would win. But another king asked for one more prophet. So they called a *prophet* named Micaiah.

Micaiah told what he had seen. He saw the LORD sitting on his throne. All the *host of heaven* stood on his right and on his left. The LORD asked who would lead Ahab to go to battle. One said one thing, and another said something else. Then a spirit came forward with a plan, and the LORD sent it.

Heiser pointed to this scene as a clear picture of the council at work. God asks, the members talk, and God decides. The members speak, but God has the last word. Micaiah's message was a warning. The story says Ahab did not listen, and he did not come home from the battle.

words.d: a person who brings a message said to come from God
a Bible phrase for the many heavenly beings around God's throne

look.title: Who Spoke to King Ahab?
rows: Prophets who said Ahab would win
look.prompt: Micaiah was one voice against about 400. Why might it be hard to be the only one who says something different?

check.q: In Micaiah's vision, who stood around the LORD's throne?
check.why: First Kings 22:19 says all the host of heaven stood on the right and left.

check.q: What did the LORD ask the host of heaven?
choices: Who would lead Ahab to go to battle
check.why: In 1 Kings 22:20 the LORD asks who will lead Ahab to go up to battle.

check.q: What did Heiser say this scene shows?
choices: God needs the council's vote to act
The council talks, and God decides
Micaiah was a member of Ahab's court
check.why: Heiser saw the scene as the council at work, with God making the final choice.

lessons.title: The Sons of God in Job
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Job opens with the sons of God coming before the LORD, including one called the satan.
reading: The Book of Job begins on earth with a good man named Job. Then the scene moves to heaven. Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD. That means they came to stand before him, like officials reporting to a king.

One member came too. The Hebrew calls him *the satan*. The word satan means adversary, or one who challenges. It has the word the in front, so it works like a title. He questions whether Job is good only because life has gone well for him.

Heiser read the satan in Job as a member of the council acting as a challenger. Much Jewish tradition sees the satan in Job as an angel who serves God as an accuser. Many Christians read him as the devil. Job 38:7 shows another scene: the sons of God shouting for joy when the world was made.

words.d: a Hebrew title in Job meaning the adversary, a member who challenges before God
someone who takes the other side or challenges you

look.title: The Sons of God Shout for Joy
look.text: God asks Job where he was when the earth was made. When its cornerstone was laid, the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.
look.cite: Job 38:4–7, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What were the sons of God doing when the world was made? How does that feel different from Job 1?

check.q: What does Job 1:6 say the sons of God did?
choices: Came to present themselves before the LORD
check.why: Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to stand before the LORD.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
check.why: Satan means adversary; in Job it has 'the' in front, like a title.

check.q: In Job 38:7, what did the sons of God do when the world was made?
check.why: Job 38:7 says the sons of God shouted for joy.

lessons.title: Isaiah and the Seraphim
lessons.mainIdea: In Isaiah 6, Isaiah sees God's throne with seraphim and hears God ask, 'Who will go for us?'
reading: Isaiah 6 begins in the year King Uzziah died, around 740 BCE. Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne. The edge of his robe fills the temple. Above him are *seraphim*. The name likely comes from a Hebrew word for burning, so it may mean burning ones.

Each seraph has six wings. With two it covers its face. With two it covers its feet. With two it flies. They call to one another: holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. The whole earth is full of his glory.

Then God asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Heiser read the word us as God speaking to his council. Other readers see it differently. Many Christians see a hint of the Trinity. Others say it is a royal way of speaking. Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me."

words.d: heavenly beings with six wings in Isaiah 6; the name may mean burning ones
set apart and completely pure; in Isaiah 6 the seraphim call God holy three times

look.title: A Seraph's Six Wings
look.prompt: How many wings in all? Why might the seraphim cover their faces near God's throne?

check.q: How many wings does each seraph have in Isaiah 6?
check.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

check.q: What do the seraphim call out?
choices: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts
Rise up and judge the earth
check.why: In Isaiah 6:3 the seraphim call God holy three times.

check.q: How did Heiser read the word us in 'Who will go for us?'
choices: As God speaking to his council
As Isaiah speaking to his family
check.why: Heiser read the us in Isaiah 6:8 as God addressing the divine council.

lessons.title: Heavenly Beings
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the gods in Psalm 82 are heavenly beings, and he gave reasons from the text.
reading: Who are the elohim that God judges in Psalm 82? Heiser said they are heavenly beings, members of God's council. He gave reasons from the text. A reason from the text is called *evidence*. Good readers look for it.

First, verse 7 says they will die like humans. Heiser asked why anyone would tell humans they will die like humans. The line makes more sense, he said, if they are not human. Second, Psalm 89 places the council in the heavens.

Third, verse 8 says God will judge all the nations. Heiser linked the council members to the nations of the world. Judges in Israel did not rule over every nation. For Heiser, these heavenly beings had been given jobs over the nations, and they did them badly.

words.d: facts or words in a text that support an answer
the peoples and countries of the world

look.title: Weighing a Clue
look.text: Psalm 82:6–7, retold: I said you are gods, children of the Most High. But you will die like humans. Heiser asked: if these listeners were already human, why would God say they will die like humans?
look.prompt: Explain Heiser's clue in your own words. Does the line make you think of humans or heavenly beings? Why?

check.q: Who did Heiser say the elohim in Psalm 82 are?
check.why: Heiser read them as heavenly members of the divine council.

check.q: Which verse says the elohim will die like humans?
check.why: Psalm 82:7 says they will die like humans.

check.q: Why did Heiser point to verse 8 and the nations?
choices: It names the judges of Israel
It proves there is no council
Judges in Israel did not rule over every nation
check.why: Verse 8 speaks of all the nations; Heiser linked the council to them, not to Israel's judges.

lessons.title: Human Judges
lessons.mainIdea: Other Jewish and Christian readers have said the gods in Psalm 82 are human judges or rulers.
reading: Heiser's reading is not the only one. Over many centuries, some Jewish and Christian readers have said the elohim in Psalm 82 are human *judges* or rulers. The reformer John Calvin, in the 1500s, read the psalm this way. Some old Jewish translations do too.

These readers have reasons as well. The psalm is about being fair in court. It talks about protecting the poor and the weak. That was the job of human judges in Israel. Rulers and judges acted for God, so these readers think the psalm could call them gods as an honor.

Readers of this view say verse 7 is a warning. You have an honored title, but you are still humans, and you will die. Both readings look closely at the same eight verses. They come to different answers about who is being judged.

words.d: people who decide cases and say what is fair
a leader in the 1500s who worked to change the church in Europe

look.title: Two Readings Side by Side
look.text: Reading A (Heiser): The gods are heavenly beings in God's council who ruled the nations unfairly. Reading B (some Jewish and Christian readers): The gods are human judges who were honored with a high title but ruled unfairly.
look.prompt: What do both readings agree on? Where do they differ? Name one clue each reading uses.

check.q: Which reformer read Psalm 82 as being about human rulers?
check.why: John Calvin, in the 1500s, read the gods of Psalm 82 as human rulers and judges.

check.q: Why do some readers think Psalm 82 is about human judges?
choices: It talks about being fair in court and protecting the poor
It takes place in Job's house
check.why: The psalm's focus on fair judging and helping the poor matches the work of human judges.

check.q: How do human-judge readers explain 'you will die like humans'?
choices: As proof the judges were angels
As a line about the sea
As a mistake in the text
As a warning that honored rulers are still humans who die
check.why: They read verse 7 as reminding rulers that they are still mortal humans.

lessons.title: Jesus Quotes Psalm 82
lessons.mainIdea: In John 10:34, Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, and readers on both sides use this passage.
reading: Psalm 82 also appears in the New Testament. In John 10, some people are upset with Jesus. They say he is claiming to be God. In John 10:34, Jesus answers with Psalm 82:6: "Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?" That is the King James Version.

In the next verse, Jesus says Scripture called them gods, unto whom the word of God came. Readers who hold the human-judge view point to this line. They say it shows the gods were humans who received God's word.

Heiser and others who see heavenly beings in Psalm 82 explain Jesus' words in a different way. The *Gospel* of John does not stop to explain the psalm. So readers keep studying this passage. It is one reason Psalm 82 is discussed so much.

words.d: one of the four New Testament books about Jesus: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
to repeat someone's exact words

look.title: Jesus Answers
look.text: Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?
look.prompt: Which psalm is Jesus quoting here? Why might two groups of readers both use this verse?

check.q: Which verse of Psalm 82 does Jesus quote in John 10:34?
check.why: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'I said, Ye are gods.'

check.q: Why do human-judge readers point to John 10:35?
choices: It says the gods were those to whom the word of God came
It says the gods were stars
check.why: They read 'unto whom the word of God came' as pointing to humans.

check.q: What is a Gospel?
choices: One of four New Testament books about Jesus
check.why: The Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, books about Jesus.

lessons.title: Comparing Readings Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: A fair reader can explain each reading, with its clues, without making fun of either one.
reading: You have now seen two ways to read Psalm 82. How can you compare them fairly? Start by saying each reading in words its own readers would agree with. Then name the clues each one uses. That is called stating a view *fairly*.

Next, check each clue in the text itself. Find verse 7. Find verse 8. Read Psalm 89:5–7 and John 10:34–35. Ask what each passage says before you ask what it means. Heiser encouraged readers to look at the words closely.

Last, remember that readers have discussed these verses for a very long time. Thoughtful people have reached different answers. You can explain what Heiser argued and what others argued. You do not need to make fun of anyone to do it well.

words.d: in a way that is honest and gives each side a full hearing
a reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: A Fair Report
look.text: Student A writes: Heiser read the gods in Psalm 82 as heavenly beings, because of verses 7 and 8 and Psalm 89. Student B writes: Heiser was right and anyone else is silly. Student C writes: Some readers see human judges because the psalm is about fair courts.
look.prompt: Which reports are fair? What would you change in the one that is not?

check.q: What is the first step in comparing two readings fairly?
choices: Say each reading in words its own readers would agree with
check.why: A fair comparison begins by stating each view the way its own readers would.

check.q: What should you ask before asking what a passage means?
check.why: The reading says to ask what each passage says first.

check.q: What is an interpretation?
choices: A reader's explanation of what a text means
check.why: An interpretation is one reader's explanation of a text's meaning.

choices: A gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head
review.why: The divine council is God's heavenly court, as in Psalm 82:1.

review.q: Which passage shows Micaiah's vision of the host of heaven?
review.why: Micaiah describes the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven in 1 Kings 22:19–23.

review.q: In which book do the sons of God come before the LORD, along with the satan?
review.why: Job 1–2 shows the sons of God and the satan before the LORD.

review.q: Which heavenly beings have six wings in Isaiah 6?
review.why: Isaiah 6:2 describes seraphim with six wings each.

review.q: Which psalm places the assembly of the holy ones in the heavens?
review.why: Psalm 89:5–7 speaks of the heavens and the assembly of the holy ones.

review.q: Why, according to Heiser, does God have a council?
choices: He needs their help to rule
He chooses to share his work with his heavenly family
He copied the idea from Ugarit
review.why: Heiser said God does not need a council but chooses to include others.

review.q: How do Heiser's reading and the human-judge reading of Psalm 82 differ?
choices: Heiser sees human rulers; the other sees seraphim
Heiser sees heavenly beings; the other sees human rulers
Both say the psalm is about Job
review.why: Heiser read the elohim as heavenly beings; others, like Calvin, read them as human judges.

review.q: In the story, what reminded Sam of Psalm 82?
choices: A city council meeting led by the mayor
A clay tablet at a museum
review.why: Sam saw the mayor leading the council and thought of God standing in the divine council.
